note: A four-chord turnaround with 7th and 9th chords: the chords counted on a key-chords tool, fretted, strummed in sixteenths, then comped over drums and bass with full shapes and then shells. The old copy in C with its Key selector is now moves (any key, 90 to 110 bpm); the backing track gives the chords as numerals so it follows the key, and the text names chords by ordinal, never by letter.

exercise.title: The {{=key}} turnaround, two ways
exercise.why: Full 7th and 9th chords fill the space and shells leave it open, so choosing between them sets how much room a voice or a melody gets.

cells.text: Below are the chords of the {{=key}} major scale, each with its number. The turnaround takes four of them: the 1st chord as a major 7th, the 6th as a minor 7th, then the 2nd and the 5th, each with a 9th on top. The 5th chord leads back to the 1st, so the four go round and round.

Press a chord box below to hear it, then fret the four shapes in order.
Practice until no change needs a look at the neck.

Press Play below to start the metronome at {{=bpm}}. After a bar of count-in, the lit box shows the chord: strum the pattern in the boxes, one bar per chord, with your hand moving through the dots.
If a change comes late, keep your strumming hand going and catch the next beat 1.

tool.pattern: D . . U . U D U D . . U . U D U

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the backing track: drums and bass, with the chord boxes lighting bar by bar. The boxes show 7th chords. Play one round with your full shapes, then a round with only a shell of each chord: its root, 3rd and 7th.
Listen for how much room opens up when you change to shells.
{{?key}}In another key the shapes sit on other frets, and the chords still come round in the same order: major 7th, minor 7th, minor 9th, 9th.
